note: Feedback for the Checks of Unit 4. The design is docs/superpowers/specs/2026-11-26-chemstudy-us-english-and-unit-1-check-feedback-design.md. Options are listed in the order they are to have on the page; the option with no message is the answer.

options.text: A square of chocolate left in a warm car goes soft and runny, then hardens again in the shade
options.message: Melting and hardening again are changes of phase. Ask whether the substance at the end is the one that was there at the start.

options.text: A slice of bread in a toaster turns brown and smells different
A wet towel hung on a line is dry by the evening
options.message: The towel dried because its water turned to vapor, which is a change of phase. Is the water a different substance afterward?

options.text: Muddy water left overnight goes clear above a layer of silt
options.message: Settling is a mixture separating. Ask whether the substances at the end are the ones that were there at the start.

options.text: A chemical change happened, because the hot platinum gave off orange light
options.message: Light counts as evidence when the change itself gives it off. Ask where the heat that made this wire glow came from.

options.text: A physical change happened, because platinum is a metal that cannot react at all
options.message: Platinum can react: a hot mixture of nitric acid and hydrochloric acid dissolves it. Judge by what was seen, not by what the metal is.

options.text: A chemical change happened, because the wire changed color twice, to orange and back
options.message: The color came and went with the heat. Compare the properties of the wire before the flame with its properties once it is cool.

options.text: Nothing points to a new substance in the wire: the flame's heat made it glow
A solid formed and the pink left the liquid, which a new substance explains best
The pink color only faded because one solution diluted the other, so nothing new formed
options.message: Dilution makes a color paler. Can it also account for the solid, and for pink turning to violet?

options.text: There is no evidence of a chemical change, because no gas formed and no heat was felt
options.message: A reaction does not have to show all four signs. Weigh the signs that were seen.

options.text: The violet solid is the pink cobalt compound coming back out of its solution unchanged
options.message: Compare the colors. And a dissolved compound comes back out when water is taken away, where this solid appeared when a solution was added.

options.text: The milky mixture has no color when a light is shone through it
options.message: A white solid of either fertilizer salt would look the same. Pick the observation that would come out differently if the solid were one of the two salts.

options.text: Left to stand, the white solid sinks slowly and forms a layer on the bottom
options.message: A solid of either fertilizer salt would settle in the same way. Pick the observation that would come out differently if the solid were one of the two salts.

options.text: The white solid, filtered off and rinsed, will not dissolve in fresh water
Stirring the bucket hard for a minute spreads the cloudiness evenly through it
options.message: Stirring would do this whether or not anything new had formed. Which observation would come out differently if the solid were one of the two salts?

slips.from: atoms balanced without the charge: 2 NH₄⁺ + 3 O₂ → 2 NO₃⁻ + 8 H⁺
slips.message: Did you balance the atoms alone? Add up the charge on each side as well: an equation can have the same atoms on both sides and still not balance.

slips.from: O atoms counted in place of O₂ molecules, or every coefficient doubled
slips.message: Did you count O atoms, or double every coefficient? The coefficient counts O₂ molecules, with the smallest whole numbers.

slips.from: the O in H₂O left out: 3 O for NO₃⁻ alone
slips.message: Did you count the oxygen in NO₃⁻ alone? Water holds oxygen too, and the coefficients are whole numbers.

options.text: Benzoic acid, sodium hydroxide and sodium benzoate
options.message: Dissolved does not always mean split into ions. Check whether each of the three is strong or weak.

options.text: Sodium hydroxide and sodium benzoate
Benzoic acid and sodium hydroxide
options.message: Check each substance on its own: is it strong, weak, or a soluble ionic compound? The label (aq) alone does not mean split into ions.

options.text: Sodium hydroxide only
options.message: Go through all four substances in the equation, one at a time: strong, weak, dissolved ionic compound, or liquid? One of them is misplaced.

options.text: Equation A
options.message: That is the molecular equation. A net ionic equation leaves out the spectator ions.

options.text: Equation B

options.text: Equation C
Equation D
options.message: Add up the charge on the left side. A solid has no charge, so the charges of its ions must cancel.

options.text: Citric acid with potassium hydroxide
options.message: Citric acid is a weak acid, so it is written whole. Would H⁺ appear in its net ionic equation?

options.text: Hydrochloric acid with trimethylamine
options.message: Trimethylamine is a weak base, so it is written whole. Would OH⁻ appear in its net ionic equation?

options.text: Hydrobromic acid with a solution of potassium nitrate
options.message: Is there a base in this pair? Check whether these four ions form anything new when they meet.

options.text: Perchloric acid with strontium hydroxide
It has no spectator ions: every ion ends up in a new substance
Ca²⁺ is a spectator ion, because calcium appears on both sides of it
options.message: A spectator ion is dissolved and separate on both sides. Look at where the calcium is on the right.

options.text: OH⁻ is a spectator ion, because hydroxide is not part of the solid
options.message: A spectator ion is the same on both sides of the equation. Look for OH⁻ on the right.

options.text: It has no net ionic equation, because carbon dioxide is not ionic
options.message: A net ionic equation can contain molecules. CO₂ is written whole because it is a gas.

That is every ion in the two boxes. Some of them are in the solid now.

slips.from: one Ba²⁺ for each PO₄³⁻, so 2 Ba²⁺ left: 2 + 8 + 6
slips.message: Did you take one Ba²⁺ for each PO₄³⁻? Use the ratio in the equation.

slips.from: the leftover Ba²⁺ alone, with the spectator ions forgotten
slips.message: Did you count the leftover ions of the solid alone? Spectator ions are still dissolved too.

options.text: Charge is not conserved: the dissolved ions now add up to +4
Silver is not conserved: the box has gained four silver atoms
options.message: Count the silver in each box, ions and atoms together. A silver ion that takes an electron is still silver.

options.text: The nitrate ions should be gone, because they are spectator ions
options.message: Spectator ions take no part in the reaction, so they stay dissolved. They do not leave the box.

options.text: Nothing is wrong: every atom in the first box is in the second
options.message: Matching atoms is one test, and not the only one. Run the rest of the checks the lesson makes on a drawing before you accept this box.

options.text: 4 CH₄ molecules still in the left bulb and 4 CO₂ molecules still in the right
options.message: Gas molecules keep moving. What happens once the valve is open and each gas can reach more space?

options.text: 8 CO molecules and 8 H₂ molecules, spread through both bulbs
options.message: Every atom is there, but in new molecules. That would be a reaction, and these two gases do not react at room temperature.

options.text: 2 CH₄ molecules and 2 CO₂ molecules in all, because the gases now have twice the space
options.message: More space means the molecules are farther apart. Does it change how many there are?

options.text: 4 CH₄ molecules and 4 CO₂ molecules, every one whole, spread through both bulbs
The Cl–Cl bonds broke, and the gas is made of separate chlorine atoms
options.message: Compare the energies. The sample took in 20.4 kJ for each mole, and breaking the bonds takes 243 kJ for each mole.

options.text: The molecules moved far apart, and every Cl–Cl bond stayed intact
Some of the Cl–Cl bonds broke, since energy was absorbed by the sample
options.message: Absorbing energy does not have to mean breaking bonds. The gas has all the chemical properties of chlorine: what does that say about its particles?

options.text: The molecules themselves grew larger as they took in the energy
options.message: Molecules do not swell when they are heated. Ask what the 20.4 kJ for each mole was used to overcome.

options.text: Water left sample 1, while in sample 2 new bonds formed, taking in atoms from the air
Both are physical changes: in each sample a liquid evaporated and left the solid behind
options.message: Evaporation takes molecules away, so the mass falls. Does that fit a sample that gained mass?

options.text: Both are chemical changes, because both paints ended up hard and dry to the touch
options.message: Hard and dry is how both ended, not what happened on the way. Check which sample a wet brush turns back into paint.

options.text: Sample 2 is a physical change, because its mass went up where sample 1's went down
options.message: A mass that goes up is not just the reverse of one that goes down. What could add mass, and can oil or water turn sample 2 back into paint?

options.text: Whole Na₂SO₄ units move apart from one another and spread through the water
options.message: Sodium sulfate is ionic. What happens to the ionic bonds between its ions when it dissolves?

options.text: One Na₂²⁺ ion and one SO₄²⁻ ion separate, and each attracts water molecules around it
options.message: Check the sodium. What does the subscript 2 in Na₂SO₄ count?

options.text: Bonds inside each sulfate ion break, freeing sulfur and oxygen atoms into the water
options.message: Dissolving does not break the covalent bonds inside a sulfate ion. They stay as they are.

options.text: Two Na⁺ ions and one SO₄²⁻ ion separate, and each attracts water molecules
Every 2 g of H₂S that reacts uses up 1 g of SO₂
options.message: Coefficients count moles, not grams. Work out the mass of 2 mol of H₂S and of 1 mol of SO₂, and compare.

options.text: For every 1 mol of SO₂ that reacts, 3 mol of sulfur atoms form
The total number of moles of substances is the same before and after the reaction
options.message: Add up the coefficients on each side. Atoms are conserved, but are moles of substances?

options.text: H₂S and SO₂ molecules are used up in equal numbers
options.message: Look at the coefficients of the two gases. They count molecules as well as moles.

That is the two masses added together. Go through moles, and find the limiting reactant.

slips.from: actual yield divided by the mass of WO₃

slips.from: stopped at the theoretical yield in kilograms

options.text: N₂H₄, because it has the most hydrogen atoms
options.message: How many hydrogen atoms a molecule has does not decide anything. Compare each reactant with what it becomes: which one has lost H⁺?

options.message: The question is about the forward reaction. Compare each reactant with what it becomes: which one has lost H⁺?

options.text: OH⁻, because hydroxide is what acids react with

Anilinium ion, C₆H₅NH₃⁺, and aniline, C₆H₅NH₂
Anilinium ion, C₆H₅NH₃⁺, and hydroxide ion, OH⁻

options.text: Aniline, C₆H₅NH₂, and hydroxide ion, OH⁻
options.message: These are the two bases of the equation. The members of a conjugate pair differ by one proton and by nothing else.

options.text: Anilinium ion, C₆H₅NH₃⁺, and water, H₂O
options.message: These are the two acids of the equation, one on each side. The members of a conjugate pair differ by one proton and by nothing else.

options.text: Conjugate acid H₃PO₄, conjugate base PO₄³⁻
options.message: Count the protons between H₃PO₄ and HPO₄²⁻. A conjugate is one proton away.

options.text: Conjugate acid PO₄³⁻, conjugate base H₂PO₄⁻
options.message: A conjugate acid has one more proton than the species it comes from. Does PO₄³⁻ have more protons than HPO₄²⁻, or fewer?

options.text: Conjugate acid H₂PO₄⁻, conjugate base PO₄³⁻
Conjugate acid H₂PO₄²⁻, conjugate base PO₄²⁻
options.message: A proton carries a charge. Adding one or taking one away changes the charge as well as the formula.

options.text: Neither side is favored, because both acids are weak

options.text: Products are favored, and CH₃NH₂ is a stronger base than CN⁻

options.message: HCN is the stronger of the two acids. What does that say about the strength of its conjugate base?

options.text: Reactants are favored, and CH₃NH₂ is a weaker base than CN⁻
options.message: Find the two acids, one on each side, and their conjugate bases. The stronger acid has the weaker conjugate base.
